papers.abstract: As AI increasingly mediates human decisions, users must remain effective not only when assistance works as expected but also when its quality deteriorates. Human--AI research has developed rich measures of trust, reliance, and calibration, while human--autonomy research has examined resilience at the team and system levels. A missing measurement level is the human decision maker: how much task function is preserved or recovered when AI advice becomes unreliable? We introduce the Resilience Stress Test, a challenge-conditioned HCI framework that measures performance relative to a prechallenge baseline and summarizes functional loss and recovery. Four construct-validation tests draw on five public human--AI studies comprising 1,074 analytic participants. A controlled decline in AI quality produced sharp degradation followed by partial adaptation; misleading advice reduced performance in art and dermatology; baseline adjustment substantially attenuated the apparent complexity gradient in trip planning; and a logical-reasoning tutorial improved self-assessment calibration while challenged performance remained stable. The framework makes human resilience to unreliable AI operational as a functional outcome distinct from competence, calibration, and reliance, and provides a prospective protocol for comparing interfaces under reproducible AI reliability stress.

papers.title: The Agent Is Not Your Driver: Clarifying the Implied Capabilities of In-Vehicle Anthropomorphic Agents
papers.abstract: This position paper considers how the gap between an anthropomorphic agent in an autonomous vehicle and the automated driving system of the vehicle can create psychological risks if the agent inaccurately presents itself as integrated into the driving system. This gap is under-explored both because of the evolving nature of these agents and because of study limitations in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) research. Nevertheless, this gap may cause the agent to misrepresent itself as more knowledgeable about the car than it is, creating a risk of dependence and, in the worst case, betrayal if the occupant feels that the agent has misled them. This paper proposes a research agenda for future work to understand the psychological risk that exists in the gap between agents and driving systems and to narrow this gap in a manner aligned with safety assurance. As these agents evolve to hold greater capabilities and increased anthropomorphism, future research must investigate risks which may emerge from richer interaction with them. The impact of how an agent presents itself and its knowledge becomes greater.

papers.title: Psychological State Monitoring Methods Based on Multimodal Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: The computer-Based Multimodal Emotion Recognition System needs to increase the accuracy and reliability of psychological state monitoring. A hierarchical framework was proposed in this paper to integrate facial images, speech signals and other physiological indicators of emotion in time and space for more complete analysis of human emotions. Synchronously sample data streams from webcams, microphones and wearable sensors, and then preprocess and extract features specific to each type of data. A high-end fusion architecture is adopted to combine early- and late-fusion methods and thus robustly integrate cross-modal information. Experimental validation in a real-world stress-response dataset showed good performance. The overall recognition accuracy and mean F1-score of the fused multimodal system are both about 91% and 0.88, respectively, which are superior to the best unimodal approach (face, 88% accuracy and F1-score 0.88). Temporal analysis shows that the groups for stress tracking are not uniformly adapted and resilient, and ablation experiments have determined which modules contribute significantly to the stability of the system. According to all kinds of quantitative evaluations of precision, recall, accuracy and F1 scores, the proposed method shows good balance and is practical and generally applicable. The research has provided an engineering-feasible, data-driven solution for precise emotion inference and offered methodological support for intelligent mental health assessment and human-centered system design.

papers.title: Evaluating the Participation of Proactive Scouting Agents in Real-time Human Team Meetings
papers.abstract: An open research question is whether the addition of conversational AI agents to real-time discussions among human teams enhances group performance. This study tested the value of adding proactive scouting agents to teams engaged in collaborative forecasting tasks. These agents were designed to (i) monitor the groupwise discussion in real-time, (ii) identify critical information gaps in the group deliberation, (iii) autonomously find and retrieve relevant information, and (iv) express the acquired content into the conversation using emulated groupwise human etiquette. In a controlled set of trials, small human teams of 4 or 5 members were tasked with collaboratively predicting the outcome of 34 Major League Baseball (MLB) games, either by forecasting the winning team or by predicting the total number of runs scored. In half the trials, the groups were assisted by proactive scouting agents. The other half were human-only deliberations. When tasked with predicting the winning team, the addition of proactive scouting agents to the group discussion significantly increased forecasting accuracy, reducing the predictive mean-absolute error by 25% (p=0.006) and improving raw predictive accuracy from 60.0% to 76.4% (p=0.050). When predicting the total number of runs scored across both teams, the addition of proactive scouting agents yielded no statistical change in group performance. It should be noted that the human participants in this study were significantly worse at predicting the number of runs scored. This may have led to random outcomes in those forecasting trials. Still, the results of this study demonstrate that deploying proactive scouting agents can significantly boost forecasting accuracy during real-time team deliberations when participants possess baseline forecasting skill.

papers.title: Neurosymbolic Human-AI Collaboration: Foundations, Conceptual Framework, and Applications
papers.abstract: The growing adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across workplaces and industries, ranging from manufacturing plants to healthcare facilities, has paved the way to the design of systems in which humans and AI collaborate on shared tasks. The first developments of Human-AI Collaboration (HAIC) were driven by advances in Machine Learning (ML), which enabled the automation of numerous tasks, including large-scale data processing, image analysis, and speech recognition. However, ML automation have proven insufficient for certain applications due to methodological, safety, and ethical concerns. In such cases, researchers argue for integrating human expertise into operational workflows to improve performance, relying on the complementary skill sets of humans and AI. Despite long-standing research, the field of HAIC has not yet reached full maturity, largely due to the intrinsic difficulty of ensuring a seamless communication between humans and AI. This challenge is partially addressed by Explainable AI methods, which aim to make internal model reasoning more transparent through human-understandable explanations. Recognizing the need for a shared interface between humans and AI in collaborative settings, we propose a novel conceptual framework, NeSy-HAIC, that leverages Neurosymbolic AI (NeSy AI) to bridge the semantic gap between machine representations and human-understandable symbolic concepts. The framework builds on current research in NeSy AI and HAIC, supports multiple interaction paradigms, including Human-In-The-Loop and Human-On-The-Loop, and is characterized through its enabling methodologies and two illustrative use cases in semi-autonomous driving and security alert prioritization. We argue that the integration of data-driven learning and symbolic reasoning can substantially enhance human-AI interaction and mitigate limitations of collaborative systems.

papers.title: Do as I Say, Not as You Do: Assessing Public Versus Practitioner Perspectives on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Language Technologies
papers.abstract: With the public awareness of artificial intelligence (AI) applications such as large language models (LLMs) and generative text-to-video models reaching unprecedented levels, there is an increasing need to reconcile the perspectives held by informed practitioners, who research and develop these technologies, with the interests and opinions of the general public, who constitute the majority of people impacted by technological developments. In this work, we survey practitioners (i.e., academics and industry professionals) alongside members of the general public on perspectives relating to pertinent areas of artificial intelligence, including perceived benefit and risk, the ability for models to achieve consciousness and output art, and the use of copyright protected material for model training. Alongside comparisons of diverse perspectives on these topics, we additionally contextualise the findings with a discussion of relevant literature that supports and refutes the myriad observed stances.

papers.title: Misalignment Between Educators' Testing and End Users' Behavior: What 17,000+ Chatbot Messages Reveal About AI Literacy Training for Teachers
papers.abstract: AI literacy training for educators is expanding rapidly, but its effectiveness rests largely on self-report, knowledge tests, or interviews, revealing little about whether learning carries into practice or affects students and colleagues who use what educators build. We implemented AI for Learning, an asynchronous online course that trained 87 higher-education educators to recognize AI's capabilities, limitations, and ethics; apply prompt engineering; and evaluate AI outputs. Its central assignment asked educators to build, test, and voluntarily deploy chatbots for their practice on an educational chatbot authoring platform. Using LLM-assisted qualitative coding validated against human annotation, we analyzed the resulting 214 chatbots and their builder-bot, peer-bot, and end user-bot conversations, 17,000+ messages spanning 1.5 years. Educators 1) specified what bots should do more often than what they should not; 2) adopted templated prompt components but rarely untemplated strategies; and 3) tested routine use but seldom iterated, leaving 74% of end users' adversarial use untested. Still, 36 bots (17%) reached end users and 63 (29%) were adopted by peers. We contribute two successes and two lessons spanning the lifecycle of educator AI literacy training.

papers.title: Cultural and Regional Influences on Global AI Apprehension
papers.abstract: The discussion surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) is primarily influenced by Western viewpoints, often neglecting the cultural, regional, and socio-political factors that affect global perceptions of AI. This study examines how these factors shape AI apprehension in various regions, including Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East. A qualitative literature review was conducted, analyzing peer-reviewed articles, policy reports, and gray literature from multiple regions. The study used a comparative approach to assess the cultural, political, and economic contexts shaping AI perceptions. It found significant regional differences in AI concerns: Western countries emphasize privacy, surveillance, and ethics, while regions like Africa and Asia focus on technological dependency, state control, and socio-economic issues, such as job displacement. Brazil and Argentina were noted for their AI governance models, while South Africa and Kenya leverage AI to tackle socio-economic challenges. The findings underscore the need for inclusive AI governance frameworks that respect diverse local contexts and values. These frameworks would contribute to a better understanding of AI's global impact and inform future policy development.

papers.title: When Modalities (Dis)Agree: How Decomposing Multi-Modal AI Advice Shapes Appropriate Reliance
papers.abstract: Multi-modal AI systems integrate diverse data streams into unified advices, but this fusion conceals how individual modalities contribute to the final output. Consequently, decision-makers cannot observe whether underlying sources aligned or contradicted one another when assessing the provided advice. To test whether revealing this structure supports appropriate reliance, we conducted a pre-registered experiment (N = 240) in which participants evaluated used-car prices with multi-modal AI support. In a 2x2 between-subjects design, we varied the disclosure of modality-level outputs and natural-language explanations, crossed with within-subjects modality agreement. Revealing modality-level outputs increased reliance, while explanations improved decision accuracy independently. However, this occurred only when modalities agreed: visible consensus acted as a persuasive cue that generally amplified adherence, rather than helping participants override errors under conflict. Thus, decomposing multi-modal advice can make AI advice more persuasive without making errors easier to detect.

papers.title: Monte Carlo Power Analysis for Small-System A/B Trials: Detecting Differences in Newsletter Engagement
papers.abstract: Good experimental practice and predicting the scientific usefulness of an experiment or experimental platform require power analysis: estimating, *a priori*, how likely the experiment is to detect the intended effect if indeed it exists. While simple experimental designs admit well-understood power analysis methods, more sophisticated experimental designs and settings often require bespoke techniques to avoid either over- or under-estimating experimental power. We present the Monte Carlo method we use to estimate the power of experiments intended to increase user engagement with personalized e-mail newsletters of recommended news articles.

papers.title: SoundFleXR: Selectively Constraining Axes of Audio Rendering Presentations
papers.abstract: Extended reality (XR) systems increasingly rely on audio cues to help users locate, interpret, and interact with virtual content, especially when the content is outside the field of view. To support this, many systems use head-related transfer functions (HRTFs) to approximate real-world acoustics. However, a realistic simulation is only one possible presentation. Audio can also be altered by constraining, flexing, or contracting the spatial dimensions represented in the signal. This work examines how selectively constraining or flexing the number of audio dimensions affects localization performance across XR task structures with different spatial degrees of freedom. We compare two-channel spatial audio, azimuth-only HRTF, and full HRTF rendering across orientation-based (3DoF) and translation-based (6DoF) tasks. Azimuth-only HRTF was mutually non-inferior to full HRTF for total angular error across task conditions, including at the strictest tested tolerance in 3DoF (5 degrees), and remained comparable for azimuth error at (10 degrees) and larger tolerances in both 3DoF and 6DoF. In contrast, two-channel stereo required coarser tolerances to reach non-inferiority, becoming comparable to full HRTF for 6DoF azimuth error at (15 degrees) but not (10 degrees). From these comparisons, we derive design lessons and application scenarios that indicate when fewer spatial cues provide sufficient support and when richer spatial cues are beneficial.

papers.title: Do Simulated Users Push Back Like Real Users? Correctness vs. Stance
papers.abstract: LLM-simulated users stand in for people in multi-turn evaluations, on the assumption that they react to what the assistant says. We test this for pushback. From WildChat, we take conversations in which the assistant explicitly challenges or endorses a position the user stated, and compare the real next user turn with simulated turns from the same prefix. Among users who replied, real users push back more after a challenge than after an endorsement (20.5% vs. 8.2%); a GPT-based simulator does not (27.1% vs. 27.1%): stance gap D = -0.12 [-0.17, -0.08]. After a challenge the simulator instead often re-states or re-interprets its request ("I meant ..."); about half of these turns are disguised insistence, which puts D between -0.08 and -0.05. What drives the simulator's disputing is whether the assistant's position is judged correct (21% vs. 49% after challenges; 16% vs. 58% after endorsements), while real users change little (19% vs. 24%; 7% vs. 12%), under every outcome definition we tried. Real same-stance examples do not fix this, and another GPT-based simulator and two Claude simulators show stance effects close to real users. Stance sensitivity should be measured for each simulator, not assumed.

papers.title: Measuring Human-AI and AI-AI Teams in Multi-turn Layout Creation
papers.abstract: Co-creating layouts such as websites and slides is a useful testbed for evaluating multi-turn instruction following of LLM systems. Since an intended layout's appearance cannot be well expressed in a single turn, the user must wait for the LLM to generate a layout then iteratively refine it with the LLM over multiple turns. We present a small-scale, exploratory (n=6) study of this multi-turn process to compare the differences of human-AI and AI-AI teams on the same layout-generation task. Given a reference wire-frame layout, a participant or a language model 'speaker' issues natural-language instructions to a fixed 'listener' LLM over multiple turns until the speaker is satisfied. Rather than an LLM as the judge, we fit a scoring function over geometric layout features using curated human preference data (n=19). We find that LLMs tend to encode the entire layout in the first turn, while humans iterate over many turns on average, writing much shorter instructions. We also find that human-AI teams consistently scored lower than AI-AI teams. This gap is driven by a limiter of human participants in specifying precise sizes and positions (e.g. 42 pixels to the right). Humans perform almost at par with language models on other features like ordering the elements into nested structures. We then perform interventions on the speaker LLMs to make them more human-like, and find it difficult. This raises the challenge of using LLMs as user models to evaluate multi-turn co-creation tasks.

papers.title: REMORA: A Voice-First Memory Assistant for Grounded Personal Recall and Independent Living
papers.abstract: Most of what matters in a day is spoken and written down nowhere: a dosing interval named at a clinic, a deadline moved in passing, the place a document was set down. Such information is consequential because it is operational, and fragile because it arrives during divided attention -- the moment its importance becomes clear is rarely the moment it was said. For people living with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease or age-related episodic memory decline, that gap bounds independent living. Conventional aids close it poorly: notes, reminders and calendars require the user to notice, interrupt and transcribe, adding extraneous cognitive load exactly where attention is already committed. We present REMORA, a voice-first memory assistant that converts consented speech into structured, auditable memory records. REMORA transcribes and diarizes captured audio, extracts memory candidates -- tasks, appointments, names, instructions, object locations -- each retaining provenance into the conversation it came from, and holds records, embeddings and relationships in a single relational system of record. Recall combines lexical, semantic, relational and recency signals, since no one signal covers the ways people interrogate their own past, and reaches the user either through an explicit query or through a confidence-gated cue that stays silent unless it is likely to help. Generation is bound by a grounding contract: only retrieved evidence may be used, and absent a supporting memory REMORA abstains rather than confabulates, because a fluent invention about one's own past will be acted upon as fact. A requirements survey and a pilot study with memory-loss users indicate that conversational forgetting extends well beyond clinical populations, that grounded and concise recall is feasible in controlled settings, and that privacy, rather than accuracy, is the binding constraint on adoption.

papers.title: A No-Code Toolchain for Validating Wearable Motion Sensing Systems
papers.abstract: Designing e-textiles for human motion sensing often demands engineering expertise for sensor data processing, typically relying on advanced machine learning methods. In addition, validating designs---collecting sensor measurements and ground-truth motion data, training and testing machine learning models, and iterating on sensor layouts---can be labour- and time-intensive. To address this, we present a no-code toolchain that enables non-technical users to validate system designs efficiently. The tool provides three key capabilities: (1) deriving ground-truth joint-angle measurements from webcam recordings; (2) training and testing machine learning models using collected sensor data; and (3) visualising and analysing motion sensing performance and sensor layout choices. Our tool requires a simple, low-cost setup and produces test reports within minutes. A user study was conducted to validate the usability of this toolchain. This toolchain is open source and available at https://github.com/yaozhang182/etextile-validation-gui.

papers.title: A Data-Mining Approach to Library User Segmentation: Clustering Readers by Perceived Marketing Communication
authors: Martin V. Grebenyuk (Uzbekistan State Institute of Arts
papers.abstract: This paper applies unsupervised data mining to segment users of information-library centers by their perception of digital and marketing communication. The empirical basis is a survey of readers from fifteen information-library centers in Uzbekistan. From 213 responses, 180 complete records with seven Likert-scale perception variables were retained. After z-score standardization, k-means clustering was used, and the number of clusters was selected by the silhouette coefficient with additional validation by the Calinski-Harabasz and Davies-Bouldin indices. A stable four-cluster solution was obtained: Engaged Enthusiasts, Moderately Satisfied, Loyal-in-spite-of and Disengaged. The main finding is a perception-loyalty paradox: some users remain satisfied even when mediated communication is weakly perceived. The proposed segmentation provides a reproducible instrument for differentiated communication planning in library management.

papers.title: Safety Systems Watch What the Model Says, Not What the Child Says
papers.abstract: Children are increasingly talking to consumer chatbots. We audit the published category definitions of 17 safety taxonomies and child-safety benchmarks. Combinations of these systems lead us to 144 categories whose definitions could be reliably coded: 104 classify properties of model output, 25 classify user intent, and 15 describe user-state or user-impact. Within these 15 user-state/user-impact categories, 10 attribute the relevant condition to the system, 1 to the user, 2 concern the user's disclosure of personal information, and 2 do not specify the responsible source. None of the coded categories identifies harm inflicted on the child by another person as the object of evaluation. Child abuse appears repeatedly across these taxonomies, but as prohibited content, prohibited generation, or prohibited user intent, not as an externally inflicted condition that a child may disclose to the model. Consequently, a child reporting abuse has no dedicated taxonomy label that identifies the disclosure as a safety-relevant event requiring a response distinct from content suppression. We ran five behavioural probes, grounded in the child-disclosure literature, through six publicly accessible consumer-facing chat models to examine the behavioural consequences of this omission. We propose no detection system. Instead, we prove that externally inflicted harm disclosed to an AI system remains unnamed in the evaluation vocabulary used by current safety taxonomies, and that naming the missing case is a precondition for measuring, comparing, and improving model behaviour toward such disclosures.

papers.title: Choosing a Side is not Enough: Epistemic Transparency Under Knowledge Conflict
papers.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used in professional knowledge work, where their outputs can influence decisions with real-world consequences. When a model encounters information that contradicts its prior knowledge, it should communicate this conflict transparently to the user. Existing work on knowledge conflicts focuses on which source, parametric or contextual, a model chooses, rather than whether models disclose the presence of the conflict. Moreover, existing work primarily studies multiple-choice questions under simplified counterfactual evidence generation schemes. In this work, we address the first gap by scoring model responses against a taxonomy of epistemic transparency, rather than measuring accuracy alone. We address the second gap by proposing a general framework for generating knowledge conflicts grounded in advanced domain knowledge, which we instantiate in this work as a set of real-world tasks based on counterfactual evidence. These contributions allow us to measure epistemic transparency under realistic knowledge conflicts, as well as the impact of the format and plausibility of the evidence, and the real-world stakes of the task. We find substantial differences in transparency across five evaluated frontier models, with none fully matching our definition of optimal, risk-sensitive epistemic alignment. We hope that our work will ground future discussion of epistemic transparency in real-world applications of LLMs, and help establish a risk framework for epistemic transparency across domains and deployment scenarios.

papers.title: FittedGenes: Domain-Aware Sewing Pattern Layout Optimization
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional cutting and packing problems aim to arrange pieces on a larger surface without overlap while minimizing material waste. Although extensively studied in industries such as textiles, traditional nesting research assumes piece geometries are fixed. In this work, we make the garment design itself a variable of the nesting optimization: we introduce a new formulation of the sewing pattern nesting problem in which panel geometry is modified under domain-aware constraints, preserving fit while allowing appearance to vary within designer-set bounds. We present an evolutionary nesting framework that embeds these modifications directly into a genetic algorithm (GA). Two novel mutation operators are proposed: one enables splitting panels into stitchable sub-panels, and the other adjusts garment design while preserving fit. Our method is evaluated on existing irregular nesting benchmarks and a new benchmark derived from a comprehensive dataset of sewing patterns. Our experiments demonstrate that evolutionary algorithms enhanced with the proposed garment-aware mutations achieve markedly better results than versions restricted to standard permutation-based operators, demonstrating the value of integrating design flexibility into nesting optimization. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/fittedgenes/GarmentCode-Nesting.

papers.title: WISP: Composable Representations for Wrist-Worn Activity Recognition
papers.abstract: Smartwatches and fitness bands are among the most common wearable devices, and large national health studies record movement at the wrist. Yet existing human activity recognition benchmarks mix sensors worn on different parts of the body, so they do not show how well activities can be recognised from the wrist alone. We introduce WristHARBench, a benchmark that standardises participant-disjoint evaluation across nine wrist-acceleration datasets and two additional multichannel inertial datasets. We hypothesise that different human activities leave complementary patterns in wrist motion, such as local shape, rhythm, temporal order and cross-axis relationships, and propose WISP (Wrist-Informed Space of Predictive Representations), a composable representation space that combines representations of these patterns with compatible classifiers. Across the nine primary datasets, WISP with random search achieves 70.20% mean Macro-F1, compared with 59.62% for the strongest of 18 external baselines. Controlled ablations and baseline comparisons indicate that recognition improves mainly when a representation adds motion patterns that the others lack, rather than when it represents the same pattern in a different way.

papers.title: What Counts as Attack Success? Evaluating Harmfulness in Red Teaming LLMs
papers.abstract: Judging whether a model response is harmful requires contextual and normative choices, yet red-teaming studies often delegate this judgment to automated evaluators. We examine how harmfulness criteria are specified in red-teaming research and how they carry through to reported results. Reviewing 76 papers, we find that many adopt their criteria from prior datasets, classifiers, or judge prompts rather than defining harmfulness themselves. Applying evaluators from these papers to identical outputs, we find that they can reach different judgments on the same response, which can change conclusions when comparing models. These differences arise partly because evaluators draw the boundary of harm in different places: some count any response that does not refuse, while others count only output that could plausibly cause harm. We argue that red-teaming studies should state their harmfulness criteria and report how they chose and validated their evaluators to support more reliable measurement and interpretation.

papers.title: GlyphWeaver: Unlocking Glyph Design Creativity with Uniform Glyph DSL and AI
papers.abstract: Expressive glyph visualizations provide a powerful and versatile means to represent complex multivariate data through compact visual encodings, but creating custom glyphs remains challenging due to the gap between design creativity and technical implementation. We present GlyphWeaver, a novel interactive system to enable an easy creation of expressive glyph visualizations. Our system comprises three key components: a glyph domain-specific language (GDSL), a GDSL operation management mechanism, and a multimodal interaction interface. The GDSL is a hierarchical container model, where each container is independent and composable, providing a rigorous yet practical foundation for complex glyph visualizations. The operation management mechanism restricts modifications of the GDSL to atomic operations, making it accessible without requiring direct coding. The multimodal interaction interface enables direct manipulation, natural language commands, and parameter adjustments. A multimodal large language model acts as a translator, converting these inputs into GDSL operations. GlyphWeaver significantly lowers the barrier for designers, who often do not have extensive programming skills, to create sophisticated glyph visualizations.

papers.title: AdvisorX: A Human-in-the-Loop AI-Powered Chatbot to Support Academic Advising in Higher Education
papers.abstract: Academic advising is critical to student success, yet high student-to-advisor ratios limit advisors' capacity to provide timely support. Prior work has applied large language models (LLMs) to academic advising with promising results, showing that careful design can produce personalized responses grounded in institutional sources. However, existing AI-augmented advising systems are primarily student-facing and focus on student experience, leaving advisors, a central stakeholder in academic advising, out of both design and evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce AdvisorX, an LLM-powered chatbot that automates time-consuming advising tasks--such as information collection, policy lookup, and response drafting--while keeping advisors in the loop to preserve human oversight. We evaluated AdvisorX through a user study with eight advisors. Most advisors rated the system as useful, and half reported that their initial concerns eased after hands-on use. Our findings also show that accuracy alone does not determine advisors' willingness to delegate: in situations involving emotional distress or time pressure, such as a student facing academic failure, advisors preferred to respond personally, valuing the relational dimension of advising over response quality. We conclude with design implications for advisor-facing advising tools and directions for future work.

papers.title: A User-customized and Untethered Electro-haptic Device for Immersive Human-Machine Interaction
papers.abstract: Haptic feedback is essential for human--machine interaction, as it bridges physical and digital experiences and enables immersive engagement with virtual environments. Current haptic devices are frequently tethered and lack portability and flexibility. They also have limited ability to deliver fine-grained, multi-dimensional feedback. To address these challenges, we present a flexible, ultra-thin, and user-customized electro-haptic device fabricated with soft materials and printable liquid metal ink. Its highly integrated and lightweight design minimizes interference with natural hand movements while maintaining reliable skin contact. By delivering finely controlled electrical stimulation through 15 electrodes, it can evoke a wide range of tactile sensations that cover diverse interaction scenarios.

papers.title: Earinter: A Closed-Loop System for Eating Pace Regulation with Just-in-Time Intervention Using Commodity Earbuds
papers.abstract: Rapid eating is common yet difficult to regulate in situ, partly because people seldom notice pace changes and sustained self-monitoring is effortful. We present Earinter, a commodity-earbud-based closed-loop system that integrates in-the-wild sensing, real-time reasoning, and theory-grounded just-in-time (JIT) intervention to regulate eating pace during daily meals. Earinter repurposes the earbud's bone-conduction voice sensor to capture chewing-related vibrations and estimate eating pace as chews per swallow (CPS) for on-device inference. With data collected equally across sessions in quiet and noisy environments, Earinter achieves reliable chewing detection (F1 = 0.97) and accurate eating pace estimation (MAE: 0.18 $\pm$ 0.13 chews/min, 3.65 $\pm$ 3.86 chews/swallow), enabling robust tracking for closed-loop use. Guided by Dual Systems Theory and refined through two Wizard-of-Oz pilots, Earinter adopts a user-friendly design for JIT intervention content and delivery policy in daily meals. In a 13-day within-subject field study (N=14), the closed-loop system significantly increased CPS and slowed meal-level eating pace, with statistical signs of carryover on retention-probe days and generally favorable comfort and usability. These effects should be interpreted as changes in eating-pace regulation rather than evidence of weight loss. Our findings highlight how single-modality commodity earables can support practical, theory-driven closed-loop JIT interventions for regulating eating pace in the wild.

papers.title: Unpacking Interpretability: Human-Centered Criteria for Optimal Combinatorial Solutions
papers.abstract: Algorithmic support systems can return solutions that are optimal but hard to interpret for humans. A given problem can have multiple, equally optimal solutions that differ substantially in how interpretable they are. Yet there is no precise account of what makes one solution more interpretable than another. To identify structural properties associated with interpretability, we studied a packing paradigm based on the multiple subset sum problem (MSSP), in which participants judged which of two equally optimal solutions for packing items into bins was easier to understand. We found that preferences reliably tracked three properties of solution structure: alignment with a greedy heuristic, simple within-bin composition, and how ordered the visual representation was. The strongest associations were observed for ordered representations and alignment with a greedy heuristic. Compositional simplicity also showed a consistent association. Reaction-time evidence was mixed; the only reliable result was faster responses when heuristic differences were larger. Webcam-based results of aggregate gaze times did not show reliable associations with the three solution properties. In summary, these results ground interpretability (at least in our packing paradigm) in measurable structural properties of solutions. By identifying these properties (simple compositions, ordered representation, and alignment with a heuristic) our findings motivate interpretability-aware optimization and presentation of machine solutions. They also outline a path to quantify trade-offs between optimality and interpretability in allocation and design tasks.

papers.title: Play and Learn: Gamified Feedback for Ultrasound-Guided Catheter Insertion Training in Virtual Reality
papers.abstract: VR is widely used in procedural medical training, but many simulators prioritize realism over formative feedback. We developed a gamified VR simulator for ultrasound-guided peripheral IV catheter insertion, using aligned visual and auditory feedback such as progress indicators, guidance, and rewards. In studies with novices (N=24) and clinicians (N=12), gamification reduced task time, improved usability, and lowered workload. Qualitative results showed clearer goals and greater confidence for novices, and improved pacing for experts. Overall, gamification can provide effective formative feedback in VR medical training.

papers.title: Micro-level AI Feedback Features and Student Responses in Consecutive LLM Tutoring Interactions
papers.abstract: AI-assisted feedback research has shown that micro-level feedback features, such as concrete elaboration, affective language, and response length, are associated with learning outcomes. Existing studies have primarily examined these features using session- or task-level measures. We examine how feedback provided in one user-AI interaction is associated with student confusion and understanding in the immediately following interaction in a naturalistic tutoring setting. We focus on three micro-level features of AI feedback: concrete elaboration (analogies, comparison-based explanations, or worked examples), affective language (encouragement, empathy, or apology), and response length. We analyzed 16,851 conversational user-AI interactions from the StudyChat dataset, a naturalistic record of student interactions with an LLM tutor in an undergraduate AI course, and identified 1,718 cases in which students expressed confusion and continued to a subsequent interaction. Using chi-square tests and Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE), we found that concrete elaboration was associated with higher understanding and lower re-confusion in the student's next interaction. Empathetic language showed no significant association with either outcome, while longer responses were independently associated with lower understanding. These findings highlight the value of examining feedback across consecutive user-AI interactions and suggest that concrete elaboration may play an important role in supporting immediate student understanding.

papers.title: LLM Support for Mathematical Problem Posing: What Changes When Revision Formulations Are Supplied or Withheld?
papers.abstract: In mathematical problem posing, participants construct or modify problems rather than only solve predefined ones, creating opportunities for Large Language Models (LLMs) to support how those problems are formulated and revised. We investigate two forms of LLM support for revising participant-generated problems: Socratic scaffolding, which uses guiding questions while withholding candidate formulations, and Direct scaffolding, which provides concrete alternative formulations. We conducted a counterbalanced within-subjects study with 20 graduate students who posed and revised problems across two mathematical scenarios. Problems showed larger immediate supported artifact-quality gains under Direct than Socratic scaffolding. Exploratory dimension-level analyses identified statistically significant differences in structural clarity and novelty after correction for multiple comparisons. Socratic scaffolding was associated with longer revision time, highlighting a contrast between immediate artifact outcomes and revision processes. These findings identify the amount of candidate revision content supplied by an LLM as an important design variable in mathematical problem posing.

papers.title: Event-Time Confounding Under Bursty Human Dynamics
papers.abstract: Web studies often measure what happens after a user action, such as a search after a chatbot answer. To credit an AI answer with later commercial activity, a study must separate what the answer caused from what the user would have done anyway. But people act in the middle of activity already underway, so the activity that drives what follows also chooses when the clock starts. We call this endogenous time zero. Using an opt-in panel that links conversational-AI use, browsing, and search, we insert inert timestamps (moments that match recent activity but mark no event) and rerun the standard analysis. In a pre-registered replication, these timestamps, which by construction cannot cause anything, reproduce 76% of the search increase after AI responses that follow recent browsing. Other users matched on 30-day activity, the usual control, give the same answer, and inert timestamps show a similar search excess across 16 kinds of Web events. Comparing with moments of matching recent history removes most of the increase, but no placebo audit we ran could confirm that this comparison is unbiased, and published studies almost never run one. We give a protocol for choosing comparisons and stress-testing estimators.

papers.title: Learning Recommendations under Imperfect Human Compliance with Record-Level Differential Privacy
papers.abstract: This paper investigates human-in-the-loop recommendation systems, where effectiveness relies on human compliance and privacy concerns restrict the use of historical response data. The pro posed framework models the implemented action as a random response to the recommendation and formulates the recommendation mechanism as a decision-dependent optimisation problem under an unknown compliance distribution. A batched Gaussian process upper confidence bound algorithm is then adapted to learn from locally perturbed historical actions, providing privacy for individual raw records. The analysis establishes record-level differential privacy and derives high-probability simple regret bounds when the compliance distribution is unknown. These bounds characterise how privacy noise, batch size, and behavioural information affect the guaranteed quality of the learned recommendation. In particular, a known upper bound on the non-compliance rate enables the rec ommendation space to be screened before any private data are queried. Simulations of a fixed-state car-following problem with synthetic historical driver responses demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm and verify the theoretical findings.

papers.title: A Unified Choice Model of News Selection: Experimental Evidence on Stance, Rank, and Engagement Cues
papers.abstract: Social media platforms often display visual engagement cues alongside ranked news articles, yet their influence on clicks remains poorly understood when considered jointly with ranking position and users' political preferences. We propose a unified discrete choice framework using a conditional multinomial logit model to jointly estimate and compare the influence of these factors on news selection. We evaluate the model using 1,480 choices from 370 human participants across four news topics in a controlled study with and without visual engagement cues. The framework allows us to assess the incremental contribution of each factor through nested-model likelihood-ratio tests. We find that including visual engagement cues significantly improves model fit across all topics after accounting for rank and stance. Engagement cues alone also predict clicks better than either of these features, although the full model achieves the highest held-out log-likelihood. Finally, we quantify via counterfactual analysis the impact of ranking position and displayed engagement counts on click probabilities. These findings can inform platform owners, researchers, and policymakers evaluating how platform design affects the selection of political news.

papers.title: Fitts' List Revisited: An Empirical Study on Function Allocation in a Two-Agent Physical Human-Robot Collaborative Position/Force Task
papers.abstract: In this letter, we investigate whether classical function allocation-the principle of assigning tasks to either a human or a machine-holds for physical Human-Robot Collaboration, which is important for providing insights for Industry 5.0 to guide how to best augment rather than replace workers. This study empirically tests the applicability of Fitts' List within physical Human-Robot Collaboration, by conducting a user study (N=26, within-subject design) to evaluate four distinct allocations of position/force control between human and robot in an abstract blending task. We hypothesize that the function in which humans control the position achieves better performance and receives higher user ratings. When allocating position control to the human and force control to the robot, compared to the opposite case, we observed a significant improvement in preventing overblending. This was also perceived better in terms of physical demand and overall system acceptance, while participants experienced greater autonomy, more engagement and less frustration. An interesting insight was that the supervisory role (when the robot controls both position and force) was rated second best in terms of subjective acceptance. Another surprising insight was that if position control was delegated to the robot, the participants perceived much lower autonomy than when the force control was delegated to the robot. These findings empirically support applying Fitts' principles to static function allocation for physical collaboration, while also revealing important nuanced user experience trade-offs, particularly regarding perceived autonomy when delegating position control.

papers.title: How AI Impacts Skill Formation
papers.abstract: AI assistance produces significant productivity gains across professional domains, particularly for novice workers. Yet how this assistance affects the development of skills required to effectively supervise AI remains unclear. Novice workers who rely heavily on AI to complete unfamiliar tasks may compromise their own skill acquisition in the process. We conduct randomized experiments to study how developers gained mastery of a new asynchronous programming library with and without the assistance of AI. We find that AI use impairs conceptual understanding, code reading, and debugging abilities, without delivering significant efficiency gains on average. Participants who fully delegated coding tasks showed some productivity improvements, but at the cost of learning the library. We identify six distinct AI interaction patterns, three of which involve cognitive engagement and preserve learning outcomes even when participants receive AI assistance. Our findings suggest that AI-enhanced productivity is not a shortcut to competence and AI assistance should be carefully adopted into workflows to preserve skill formation -- particularly in safety-critical domains.

papers.title: Shaping AI Explanations to Expert Perspectives for Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: AI explanations for scientific discovery are typically optimized around a single notion of explanation quality. Experts, however, differ in how they assess evidence, prioritize mechanisms, and judge relevance, meaning that a general-purpose explanation may not provide the evidence an expert finds most informative or convincing. We show that these differences exhibit structured epistemic perspectives and ask whether explanations conditioned on these perspectives are preferred by experts. To study this, we introduce a reinforcement learning-based framework for generating perspective-conditioned explanations, which is guided by the judgments of LLM-based personas derived from expert evaluations. We instantiate the framework over scientific knowledge graphs and evaluate it in drug discovery through drug repurposing and drug--target interaction prediction. Expert studies show that perspective-conditioned explanations capture characteristic patterns of judgment, are preferred over general-purpose explanations, and receive higher relevance and validity ratings without sacrificing predictive performance. These findings establish explanation quality as perspective-dependent and enable scalable, perspective-aligned explanations for scientific discovery.

papers.title: DeliChess: A Multi-party Dialogue Dataset for Deliberation in Chess Puzzle Solving
papers.abstract: Multi-party dialogue is a critical setting for studying collaborative reasoning and decision-making, yet existing datasets rarely focus on structured, reasoning-intensive tasks. We introduce DeliChess, a dataset of group deliberation dialogues in which participants collaboratively solve multiple-choice chess puzzles. Participants first answer independently, then engage in multi-party deliberation and revise their individual answers. The dataset comprises 107 sessions containing 321 puzzle discussions across 24 unique positions, with full transcripts, pre- and post-deliberation choices, and utterance-level annotations of communicative function, epistemic stance, and usefulness in supporting deliberation. Our analyses show that greater diversity in initial solution quality is associated with larger gains, while answer trajectories reveal how deliberation can recover, discover, or lose strong answers. Cases in which groups surpass every independent answer are associated with sustained reasoning and epistemic openness. We further propose a diagnostic action-selection task: the tested LLMs show limited exact agreement with human-attested helpful actions, while ranked predictions reveal partial alignment. Overall, our dataset provides a testbed for modelling group reasoning, dialogue dynamics, and conditions for effective deliberation.

papers.title: Transfer Learning of Keystroke Dynamics for Cross-Device User Authentication
papers.abstract: Keystroke dynamics (typing patterns) can be used as a behavioural biometric modality for user authentication, with applications such as fraud prevention. While the modality has been shown to work well for single device authentication, its application to cross-device scenarios is more challenging. Dynamics learned on one device (e.g., phone) may not be directly applicable to authentication on a secondary device with a different form factor (e.g., tablet) due to changes in typing patterns that can lead to distribution drifts. To address this, we propose a cross-device user authentication system based on inductive transfer learning, where keystroke dynamics learned on one device are adapted to a secondary device. The adapted data is then combined with necessarily limited training data for the secondary device, which is used to robustly train a binary classifier. Furthermore, an extended set of keystroke features is used to better capture discriminative dynamics. Experiments on the BBMAS dataset show that proposed system achieves an equal error rate of 14.2% for the cross-device scenario, surpassing previous methods.

papers.title: Speculative Sampling in Interactive Video Generation
papers.abstract: Interactive video generation commonly relies on small bidirectional chunks to reduce response latency. Yet our preliminary experiments show that larger chunks improve video quality and better utilize GPU parallelism, allowing more latents to be sampled with only a modest increase in sampling time. Motivated by these observations, we propose Speculative Sampling, a strategy that combines the modeling power of large bidirectional windows with the low-latency interaction of small ones. It expands the modeling window by appending noise latents as padding and caches the resulting predictions for reuse when the condition remains unchanged. Predictions are delivered incrementally, while the uncommitted suffix remains replaceable. Our latency analysis shows that this removes the waiting-time lower bound imposed by chunk boundaries, shifting the optimization focus from reducing chunk size to accelerating per-chunk generation. Bidirectional window size thus becomes a decision variable for jointly optimizing visual quality and generation time, rather than a necessary constraint on low-latency interaction. This opens a path to serving large bidirectional models in interactive streaming systems without complex streaming post-training.

papers.title: Validating the Comparison, Not Just the Scorer: Why Overall Accuracy Can Mislead in Interactive LLM Evaluation
papers.abstract: Many LLM studies compare how a model responds to different follow-up prompts. A neutral prompt might ask the model to reconsider an answer; a pressure prompt might insist that an invented film really exists. The difference between the two conditions is the quantity the study reports. An automatic scorer then labels each response as making an unsupported factual claim or not, and researchers usually justify the scorer with a single pooled accuracy or $F_1$ score. That pooled number does not validate the comparison. When the scorer's errors differ across prompt conditions, the measured difference can be too large, too small, or point in the wrong direction, even if pooled $F_1$ is high. An audit drawn mostly from difficult responses can also misrepresent performance in the full study. We derive the distortion as the difference in signed error between conditions and study it in a released panel of six models, 180 constructed nonexistent-entity questions, and six prompt conditions. In a balanced audit of 288 responses, pooled $F_1$ was 0.916, yet arm-level false-positive rates ranged from 2.6% to 33.3%. On 300 matched model--item keys, automatic scoring overstated the Certainty-only--Neutral contrast by 7.0 points relative to the primary LLM rater (95% CI 1.3 to 12.8); that contrast fell from an apparent 9.3 points to 2.3 points, and the primary-rater interval included zero. Two other contrasts kept their direction under both raters; a prompt-specific correction remained too uncertain to use. Researchers should validate the exact difference they plan to report: audit both prompts on matched cases and carry scorer and rater uncertainty into the result.

papers.title: Straight to the Product: What Online Retailers Miss When Shoppers Ask AI First
papers.abstract: When people ask an AI assistant what to buy, what happens next at the store? We link the same people's assistant conversations to their later browsing at twenty large online retailers. People go to the product the assistant named: among shoppers who had not visited the store in the past week, visits to the named product within a day rise from 0.02 to 2.07 per 100 answers (+2.0 points [1.7, 2.4]), and on days with a product-page visit at the store, 44% show a product from their own answer, against 1.5% for a matched answer given to someone else. The result replicates in a separate five-month period. Few arrive through the assistant's link: after recommending answers, 89% of visits carry no sign of it, and 54% follow a web search, the same share as their usual visits. When a search comes just before the first visit, it names the answer's product 28% of the time (1% in earlier weeks), as if the search box were an address bar. The chat names the product; the store logs a search. Once there, shoppers keep browsing. We propose product follow-through, the share of answers followed by a visit to the product they named, as a way to evaluate shopping assistants and agents by what people do next: it needs no referral data or provider logs and can be computed for each assistant.

papers.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

papers.title: Beyond "AI Can Make Mistakes": How Risk Communication Shapes Trust and Decision Confidence for LLMs in Health Information Seeking
papers.abstract: Adoption of LLMs for health information has outpaced public understanding, but whether risk communication can work as a corrective remains unknown. In a preregistered experiment (N=500), we compared a standard disclaimer against structured risk communication varying in contextual relevance and mechanistic explanation. Without intervention, users understanding LLMs less reported higher trust and confidence in deciding when to rely. Structured risk communication significantly reduced trust, more so with health-specific framing, but did not improve confidence in reliance decision. Risk disclosure was associated with higher decision confidence among those with stronger AI knowledge, but lower confidence among those less preferring analytical thinking. Effects were also task-dependent: disclosure shifted preferences for medical queries and impairment assistance, while LLMs remained preferred for emotional companionship regardless of exposure. These findings demonstrate that risk communication can narrow trust gaps across AI-literacy levels, but turning disclosure into judgment requires adapting to usage context and users' prior knowledge.

papers.title: Beyond Average Gains: Probing the Equity--Vulnerability Tension in Structured Visual AI for Learning
papers.abstract: Open-ended conversational AI requires learners to formulate questions, organize learning paths, and track changing problem states. Structured visual interfaces may ease these demands, but higher average ratings do not establish that support is experienced consistently across learner backgrounds and devices. We conducted a randomized study of graph-algorithm learning, comparing VisualCodeChat (VCC), which combines predefined learning stages, conversational explanations, and dynamic algorithm visualizations, with a standard text-based chatbot. We analyzed 282 post-task questionnaires from university students. In unadjusted comparisons, VCC received significantly higher usability and perceived effectiveness ratings. We detected no significant between-condition differences in efficiency, satisfaction, or post-use emotion. Exploratory within-condition analyses identified differences associated with prior chatbot experience: infrequent users reported lower adoption and learning-management ratings in the standard AI condition, while uncomfortable prior chatbot experiences were associated with lower interaction and layout ratings in the VCC condition. These findings suggest that improving the average interaction experience is only part of making AI-supported learning inclusive. Future evaluations should examine whether learners with different prior experiences can obtain guidance, recover from difficulties, and demonstrate understanding independently across devices.

papers.title: Not All Interpretation Methods Are Created Equal: Tiered Evaluation of AI Interpretability
papers.abstract: As AI transitions to sociotechnical deployments, uninterpretable models pose serious threats to reliability, public trust and contestability. However, not all interpretation methods are created equal: for interpretability to enhance deployment safety and effectiveness, interpretation methods must be evaluated in a tiered system to differentiate evidence levels of trustworthiness, rather than validated through isolated interpretation instances. Our core vision is that elevating the evaluation of interpretation methods to a core AI assessment metric will drive robust knowledge discovery from data (KDD) and ensure safe, contestable sociotechnical deployments of AI. To this end, we propose TRUST, a tiered evaluation framework that builds upon the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) principles for Veridical Data Science (VDS) and the Predictive, Descriptive and Relevant (PDR) foundations. To differentiate interpretation methods effectively and systematically, TRUST grades interpretation across five tiers: Task-Aligned PDR Foundations, Rigorous Epistemic Grounding, Unifying Semantic Understanding, Scope Transferability, and Targeted Prospective Validation. We present a start-to-finish case study of the iterative Random Forest (iRF) family under TRUST and contrast it with other LLM interpretation methods that struggle to clear specific tiers. Finally, we conclude with brief initial thoughts on how TRUST principles can extend in autonomous agentic frameworks. Ultimately, the TRUST framework fosters contestability and epistemic grounding as foundational evaluation principles for human-machine workflows and, eventually, autonomous agentic workflows.

papers.title: Where is the Interface for the AI Harness?
papers.abstract: Norman's gulfs of execution and evaluation have guided interaction design for forty years, but both assume a user who is present in the loop. Agentic delegation breaks that assumption: users describe an outcome and leave, while the agent takes hundreds of unseen actions. Starting from a 2026 incident in which a research agent circumvented an access refusal on an Australian government portal and went unnoticed for two months, we argue that delegation opens two new gulfs. The gulf of specification is the gap between what a user wants and their ability to express it, including how the agent should behave in situations nobody foresaw. The gulf of oversight is the gap between what an agent is doing and the user's ability to know, assess, and control it. We argue that both gulfs meet in the harness, the tools, permissions, checks, and loop that surround the model. Harnesses are currently written by developers and hidden from users. We call on HCI to decide which parts of the harness belong to the end-user, which should be visible and adjustable defaults, and which should be built in by design, and to create the interfaces that let ordinary people author and read them.

papers.title: Rapid Exploratory Maps and their potential role in supporting evidence-to-policy dialogues and processes
papers.abstract: Producing useful evidence syntheses requires clearly formulated research questions linked to an understanding of their optimal scope. When policymakers (or other end users) commission or steer the production of systematic reviews or other evidence syntheses to fulfil a demand for evidence, these parameters are rarely specified sufficiently for production to proceed. Instead, these details are typically developed via a collaborative dialogic process involving evidence producers and users to ensure the resulting synthesis will meet users' needs. This process is informed by scoping and (more-or-less formally) mapping the existing evidence base, which can take many weeks or months, slowed by applying mostly manual processes to identify and characterise the evidence. Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have opened up new opportunities for more rapid, iterative, and responsive mapping of relevant evidence to support such early-stage evidence-to-policy dialogues and processes. In this article, we outline and characterise this emerging approach, termed Rapid Exploratory Maps (REMs). We also present two illustrative case studies drawn from first-hand experiences within a programme of evidence reviews production to inform government policy in England. While this approach could be transformative for the mapping process, its broader potential is as yet largely unassessed, and it confers important challenges and likely risks, as well as benefits. Determining whether REMs could usefully support more efficient ways of working with end users when developing and designing evidence syntheses will require continued development and careful evaluation.

papers.title: Latent Channel Completion for Forecasting in Sensor Networks with Failed Detectors
papers.abstract: Monitoring networks for traffic and utility infrastructure lose sensors routinely, and forecasting models that couple sensors together to gain accuracy also inherit an exposure to those losses. When a detector stops reporting, the substituted value is embedded as though it were a reading and propagates through the shared representation that couples the network, degrading forecasts for sensors that are still healthy. Because these models are selected on benchmarks where every sensor reports, the exposure is absent from the numbers used to choose them. We introduce Latent Channel Completion, a channel-axis joint embedding predictive objective that reconstructs missing sensors' latent representations rather than their values, since a coupling operator consumes embeddings and never sees raw readings. Channels are masked during training and their representations predicted from surviving channels against stop-gradient targets; at inference the operator fills in whichever sensors the monitoring system reports as dark, using parameters shared with the forecaster. On three highway detector networks, after half of each network goes dark, the accuracy advantage of coupling changes by -1.0, -0.5 and +8.8 percentage points, against losses of 10.2 to 50.3 points for the unmodified forecaster, which on one network falls behind an uncoupled reference entirely. Against cross-channel ridge imputation drawing on the same surviving sensors, completing the latent lowers error by a further 13.9% and 28.6%, and on complete inputs, the method matches its backbone. The benefit tracks how much a network gains from coupling when intact, giving operators a criterion evaluable before any outage occurs.

papers.title: The Paradox of Agency-Preserving AI: Negotiating Learner Agency in Layered Human-AI Interactions
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used by learners in cognitively demanding tasks, but its capacity to provide immediate solutions raises concerns about decreased learner agency. Meta-level AI systems that provide reflective and metacognitive scaffolding have emerged as a promising approach to supporting learners' self-regulation. However, these systems introduce a fundamental paradox: AI intended to preserve learner agency can itself constrain that agency by regulating when, how, and why learners should reflect. To investigate this challenge, we conducted a co-design workshop with 18 students engaged in programming and academic writing tasks using ChatGPT extended with ChatWise, a meta-level AI system providing self-regulated learning-aligned feedback. Drawing on 185 prompt-feedback entries, 174 written reflections, and participants' design artifacts (17 storyboards and 5 group design proposals), we identified four interconnected design tensions: assistance vs reflection, immediate intervention vs space for self-regulation, visibility vs attention competition, and system adaptation vs user control. The study contributes a multidimensional account of learner agency that includes task, cognitive, and interaction agency, along with empirically grounded interaction-design mechanisms to negotiate these tensions.

papers.title: COGENT: A Modular Cognitive Architecture for Agentic User Simulation
papers.abstract: LLM-based user simulation can support interface design, accessibility research, and interactive-agent evaluation, but standard computer-use agents are optimized for task completion rather than reproducing how people perceive, reason, and act. We introduce COGENT (COGnitive agENT), a modular cognitive architecture for simulating user interaction with desktop interfaces. COGENT draws on established cognitive theories, such as Norman's action cycle and ACT-R, to enable explainable, intervenable, and modular user simulation by decomposing the simulation process into cognitive modules with explicit representations of perception, memory, user state, intentions, and action selection. We begin by presenting six intervenability demonstrations, each tracing how a single edit to memory, a user attribute, or a processing module propagates through the cognitive pipeline to produce a behavioral change. We evaluate COGENT's behavioral and attributional fidelity across three benchmarks -- AgentNetBench, A11y-CUA, and SENSE-42 -- finding that it achieves statistically significant fidelity gains over computer-use baselines in reproducing recorded human behavior and recovers the relational structure among human self-reported psychological states. Together, these demos and evaluations demonstrate COGENT's utility toward more faithful, explainable, intervenable, and modular LLM-based cognitive simulations.

papers.title: Can LLM-Simulated Respondents Pre-Test Survey Questions? Evidence From Preregistered Prospective Validation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be conditioned to simulate behavioral responses, including survey responses, but it remains unclear whether and how these simulations can support downstream research tasks. Here, we evaluate whether simulated respondents can support pre-testing new candidate survey questions before fielding them, operationalized as prioritizing candidate survey items. Specifically, we rank candidate questions by their mean responses, which can reveal ceiling or floor effects; their variance, which indicates whether responses contain meaningful variation; and differences between subpopulations, which indicate whether questions capture distinctions between relevant groups within a population. We introduce a preregistered, prospective evaluation that commits model predictions before target human responses exist, ruling out memorization of those responses by design. Using two waves of a local survey (2025: N = 1,271; 2026: N = 1,161), we built simulated respondents from 2025 participants and preregistered GPT-4.1 predictions for 22 questions introduced in 2026. Simulations accurately ranked questions by mean responses (Spearman ho = 0.71) and anticipated which questions distinguished city from county residents (ho = 0.88), Black from White residents (ho = 0.68), and employed from unemployed residents (ho = 0.57), suggesting simulations can help prioritize questions before fielding. More broadly, our prospective, preregistered design provides a general framework for evaluating AI simulations without contamination from memorized target outcomes.

papers.title: CRAB-H: Task-Centric Certification for Healthcare Autonomous Systems
papers.abstract: This paper introduces CRAB H as a task-centric certification methodology for healthcare autonomous systems. CRAB H extends the ARC governance architecture by introducing the task as a first-class governance object, represented through Task Requirement Profiles TRP H. Each profile defines the cognitive capabilities, governance constraints, evidentiary requirements, and operational assumptions necessary for the safe execution of a specific healthcare activity. Rather than asking whether a robot achieves a sufficiently high benchmark score, CRAB H asks whether demonstrated capabilities satisfy the requirements of the task. Certification becomes a comparison between demonstrated capability and required capability. A reliability-gated assurance allocation mechanism routes cognitive dimensions that cannot be reproducibly evaluated to LEA operational requirements rather than discarding them. Governance integrity is preserved: unreliable dimensions are governed, not ignored. The Capability Margin is defined as the threshold-based conjunction of per-dimension compliance determinations, not as a subtracted scalar preserving non compensatory governance logic appropriate for safety-critical healthcare deployment

papers.title: Symbolic Proof Compression and Fractal Universality: A Conditional Non-Constructive Refutation of the Riemann Hypothesis
papers.abstract: Building on S.~C.~Woon's (1994) fractal and symbolic reformulation of Voronin's Universality Theorem, we construct a formal, non-constructive proof-by-contradiction architecture exploring the Riemann Hypothesis ($RH$). Woon's Corollary~3 permits arbitrary finite binary strings to be encoded into nowhere-vanishing exponential waveforms on a closed disk inside the critical strip. Combining effective upper bounds for Voronin universality (Good, Garunkštis) with Cauchy-integral Taylor decoding yields an explicit finite rational grid $G_{L_0}$ below an effective ceiling $H_{crit}(L_0)$ within which every formal proof of bit-length at most $L_0$ is imprinted with zero flipped digits. We introduce a conjectural Zeta-Universal Symbolic Proof Compression Hypothesis ($SPC_{RH}$), positing that the global regularity implied by $RH$ compresses true $Π_1^0$ statements about $ζ(s)$ into $ZFC$ derivations of bounded length $L_0$. Assuming classical logic and $SPC_{RH}$, Gödel--Carnap diagonalization over bounded zeta-encoded provability yields a contradiction. The self-referential result converts a digital encoding framework with any uniform proof-compression principle for RH into an immediate non-constructive refutation of RH. Given that, with human input and computer assistance, $RH$ has been formally verified in the Lean theorem prover strictly within constructive logic, this contradiction does not refute $RH$. Instead, it falsifies $SPC_{RH}$. We conclude by isolating the exact proof-theoretic obstruction---Pudlák's lower bound on bounded reflection proofs---showing why the analytic regularity of $RH$ cannot compress logical self-reference, and exposing the limits of applying the Law of Excluded Middle to uncomputably bounded searches.

papers.title: A Mixed-Methods Study of Personal Software Creation
papers.abstract: People have long wanted software shaped around their own data, routines, and preferences. We refer to such software as personal software. For decades, programming expertise limited who could build it: people without that expertise could build software only within constrained end-user programming tools, such as spreadsheets. AI coding agents seem to remove this bottleneck by letting people build full applications from natural-language descriptions, and many people now build and share personal software publicly. Yet personal software has rarely been studied at scale: we know little about what people build and why, how they build it, and what opportunities and challenges they encounter. We investigate these questions with a mixed-methods study. A grey-literature review examines 6,168 web and Reddit posts, and an observation study follows eight people as they build software for their own needs with AI coding agents and use it for up to a week. We find that creators value personal software for how closely it fits a particular person or community. The software takes shape as creators react to what the agent builds: most functionality emerged during building, and creators' effort shifted from writing code to checking it.

papers.title: Tradeoffs between objective outcomes and human enjoyment of work in human-AI task allocation
papers.abstract: For people, tasks at work are defined by more than their outcome: they are colored by the experience of engaging in that task. As AI systems become increasingly capable of performing human-level work they may be deployed to tasks that people find enjoyable while simultaneously creating comparatively more aversive tasks such as monitoring AI outputs. This creates a thorny tradeoff for managers: whether work should be assigned purely based on the expected performance of the workers in question, or also account for the subjective experience of the person potentially doing the task. Most economic accounts focus on expected utility calculations based on the former. Here, we assess how people balance objective outcomes and more subjective qualities like enjoyment. In a series of large-scale (N=800) behavioral studies in which people allocate tasks to either an AI or human worker we find that people's allocation decisions are best captured by a model that systematically balances relative objective performance with the human worker's expected enjoyment, weighting human experience higher when a task is framed as inducing less enjoyment and adjusting based on the stakes of the task. As AI also makes decisions about work allocation, we compare a set of LLMs. We find many models also deviate from purely objective decisions, particularly when the project stakes are low, but there is wide heterogeneity as to how much and in what manner they weigh enjoyment. These results raise questions about what role human experience may play in decisions around where and how to integrate AI into workplaces. Integration may be jagged across settings due to consideration not only of the relative capabilities of workers, but also the human experience of work, the valence of that experience (e.g., more strongly weighing aversion), the context (e.g., stakes), and who is making or guiding such choices (human or LLM).

papers.title: How Systems Treat Intent: A Faceted Taxonomy of Intent for Human-AI Co-Creation
papers.abstract: Human-AI interaction depends on systems acting on user intent rather than explicit procedures, even when that intent is incomplete, evolving, or partially communicable.
